headline: Housatonic Water Works pauses treatment project as Great Barrington weighs takeover
dek: The private utility says a fiscal crisis has put its manganese-treatment construction on hold, while town officials work to preserve emergency water service and continue a possible municipal acquisition.
body: Great Barrington’s emergency water fight has entered a new phase. The town is still working to keep service running for Housatonic Water Works customers, but a treatment project that was supposed to address the system’s manganese problems is now on hold. The development leaves the private utility facing immediate financing pressure while the town and state agencies try to keep an emergency connection operating and consider who should control the system in the future.

The company’s construction pause was reported by The Berkshire Edge after HWW filed a Sept. 30 report with the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities. HWW Treasurer James Mercer said the company’s financial condition and negative cash flow, worsened by a payment dispute with the Great Barrington Fire District, meant it could not draw on existing loan facilities to pay for the manganese-treatment project. The company said the work is paused indefinitely while it seeks rate relief. The [Berkshire Edge report](https://theberkshireedge.com/housatonic-water-works-puts-manganese-treatment-plant-construction-on-hold-demands-emergency-rate-increase-from-dpu/) described the filing and the company’s position; the DPU has not been described as approving the requested increase.

HWW’s request comes after a 2024 DPU rate decision that allowed customer rates to rise by 90% over five years, according to The Berkshire Edge, with completion of capital projects including the treatment plant tied to that agreement. The company now says it needs an emergency increase to restore positive cash flow, cover amounts owed to the Fire District and continue necessary work. Those are HWW’s claims in filings and letters, not an independent finding that the requested rate change is warranted.

The company’s attorneys have also suggested accelerating a possible sale of HWW’s assets to the town. Under the proposal described by The Berkshire Edge, Great Barrington could assume the company’s debt and pay nothing for the franchise, property and corporate rights. That is a proposal, not a completed transaction or a purchase price set by regulators. The town’s existing valuation proceeding with the DPU remains active, and the town says it is evaluating legally and financially responsible options for a long-term solution.

The immediate operational problem is the temporary connection between HWW and the Great Barrington Fire District. In an Oct. 1 statement, the town said the connection is supporting HWW while the company addresses filtration problems in its own system. Continued use requires an agreement for continuous service between HWW and the Fire District, and Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection officials told the town that MassDEP cannot compel the Fire District to keep supplying HWW through the link. MassDEP will not approve continued use until the two entities reach an agreement and HWW incorporates that agreement into its operating procedures, the town said.

If the connection ends and HWW cannot otherwise meet the requirements of a Sept. 15 MassDEP order, the company is required to provide one gallon of bottled water per person per day to affected customers, according to the [town’s public statement](https://www.townofgb.org/m/newsflash/home/detail/224). That is a contingency in the order, not an announcement that the system has already switched to bottled-water distribution. Great Barrington said it is coordinating with MassDEP on logistics in case service is interrupted and is prepared to assist state agencies if residents need help.

The treatment project matters because it was intended to address recurring discoloration associated with manganese. MassDEP said in June that a 2025 consent order required HWW to complete the plant by June 1 after an earlier March 1 deadline was extended. HWW sought another extension, but MassDEP denied it and demanded $2,500 in partial payment from a suspended penalty. The [MassDEP notice](https://www.mass.gov/news/massdep-penalizes-housatonic-water-works-company-for-failure-to-comply-with-consent-order) said the penalty cannot be passed on to ratepayers and that the agency would continue tracking compliance.

HWW serves more than one community. The state’s [water-distribution-company directory](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/water-distribution-companies) lists 847 connections for Housatonic Water Works in parts of Great Barrington, Stockbridge and West Stockbridge. The company says it has served the area since 1897 and provides water to Housatonic village and surrounding neighborhoods. Earlier reporting by WAMC, based on an interview with Berkshire Eagle reporter Talia Lissauer, described discolored water and about 16 miles of aging pipe that ultimately need replacement. The [WAMC report](https://www.wamc.org/news/2026-09-03/mass-utility-company-faces-scrutiny-residents-face-chronic-issues-with-discolored-water) said Lissauer was aware of no health impacts from the discoloration, while residents continued to seek a durable fix.

Residents have some financial help while the dispute continues. Great Barrington’s reimbursement program can cover eligible bottled-water purchases, laundry costs and filters or other filtration products, with reimbursement capped at $1,500 per household. Customers who previously received money may apply for additional funds up to the new maximum, the town says on its [Housatonic Water Works information page](https://www.townofgbma.gov/371/Housatonic-Water-Works-Information-Resou). The program recognizes costs residents have incurred, but it does not resolve the utility’s financing, treatment or emergency-connection problems.

The next near-term test is whether HWW and the Fire District can document continuous emergency service that satisfies MassDEP. Beyond that, regulators and town officials must decide how to finance the unfinished treatment plant, address the distribution system and move the valuation process forward. Great Barrington says it will provide more updates as information can be released. For customers, the stakes are practical: the taps need to keep running now, while the legal and financial decisions that could make the system reliable for the long term remain unresolved.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Housatonic Water Works treatment project paused
seoDescription: Housatonic Water Works says a fiscal crisis paused its manganese-treatment project as Great Barrington works to preserve emergency service and weigh a possible takeover.
